pl-l3d31c1-d1e115.summary: Introduces the view that charity once had cannot be lost and that none of the damned ever had it, supported by the testimonies that follow.
claims: Some hold that charity once had cannot be lost.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e118.summary: Gives the first testimony: Paul says charity never fails.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e127.summary: Adds Augustine: charity that can be abandoned was never true.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e137.summary: Adds Augustine: charity is the proper and singular fount of the good, which no stranger shares; strangers are those who will hear 'I do not know you', so the damned do not share in this fount.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e149.summary: Adds Augustine on 1 John: when charity is rooted, be secure; no evil can come from it.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e161.summary: Adds Gregory: love is strong as death, since it utterly kills in the mind it seizes the love of the world.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e178.summary: Adds Augustine on 1 John: the invisible anointing is charity, a root that cannot wither in the burning sun but is nourished by it.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e190.summary: Adds Bede on John: the Spirit always remained in the Lord, while in the saints, as long as they are mortal, he always remains in part, that they may persist in good acts and have the virtues, and in part withdraws for a time, so that they do not always have the power of healing, raising the dead, or prophesying.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e202.summary: Adds Gregory: in the hearts of the saints the Spirit remains always in the virtues necessary for life, and comes and goes in those that display holiness, such as miracles.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e212.summary: Adds Ambrose: charity that deserts in adversity is feigned.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e221.summary: Notes that these seem to imply charity once had is not lost, leading some to the bold claim that the damned never had charity and that no one can lose it once had. Reason and authority defeat them: some are good for a time and later bad, and vice versa. So Christ says the names of some who later turned back were written in the book of life: written not according to foreknowledge, but according to present justice, of which they were then worthy.
claims: Some are good for a time and later bad.
Names are written in the book of life by present justice, not only foreknowledge.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e233.summary: Confirms with Ambrose: grace was given to some for use, like Saul, Judas, and disciples told their names were written in heaven who later turned back; this was said because of the justice they then served. Often the bad become good and the good become and remain bad, which is how names are said to be written in and erased from the book of life.
claims: Grace was given to some who later fell, such as Saul and Judas.
Names are written and erased according to present justice.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e248.summary: Begins the reply to the authorities: Paul's 'charity never fails' (sentence continues).

pl-l3d31c1-d1e257.summary: Completes the reply: Paul's saying does not support them, since he shows charity's dignity: it does not fail because it remains here and in the future, while faith, hope, and knowledge will be done away.
claims: 'Charity never fails' refers to charity's remaining in the future life.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e260.summary: Replies to Augustine's 'never true': it refers not to the essence but to the efficacy of charity, since charity that is abandoned does not make one truly blessed or lead to the true good.
claims: Charity that is lost was true in essence but not in efficacy.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e267.summary: Replies to the fount argument: the damned do not share in it at the end, since they do not persevere.
claims: The damned lack charity at the end because they do not persevere.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e270.summary: Offers an alternative: these and other sayings can be understood of perfect charity, which only the perfect have and which once had is not lost; but the beginnings of charity sometimes grow and sometimes fail. There are beginnings, progress, and perfection of virtue, as the parable of the growing seed shows. So perfect charity is rooted beyond loss, but beginning and advanced charity can be lost and often is; yet while possessed it does not allow its possessor to sin mortally.
claims: Beginning and advancing charity can be lost.
While charity is possessed, one does not sin mortally.

pl-l3d31c1-d1e279.summary: Confirms with Augustine: cupidity is the root of all evils and charity the root of all goods; both cannot be together, and one must be uprooted for the other to be planted.

pl-l3d31c1.summary: Rejects the view that charity once had cannot be lost and that none of the damned ever had it. Its proponents cite Paul ('charity never fails'), Augustine (charity that can be abandoned was never true; charity is the proper fount of the good; rooted charity produces no evil), Gregory, Bede and Gregory on the Spirit remaining in the saints, and Ambrose (feigned charity deserts in adversity). Reason and authority defeat this: some are good for a time and later bad, and Christ calls names written in the book of life that later turned back, written by present justice, not foreknowledge, as Ambrose says of Saul and Judas. Paul speaks of charity's dignity, remaining in the future; 'never true' refers to its efficacy, not its essence; the damned do not share the fount at the end, since they do not persevere. Alternatively, these sayings concern perfect charity, which cannot be lost, while beginning and advancing charity can be lost, though while possessed it does not allow mortal sin.
claims: Charity once had can be lost.
Some of the damned once had charity.
Names are written in the book of life by present justice and by foreknowledge.
'Charity never fails' refers to its remaining in the future life.
Perfect charity cannot be lost, but beginning and advancing charity can.
While charity is possessed, it does not allow mortal sin.
